why_this_tool: The lesson's verified documentation covers the whole RAG pipeline on one managed vector database, from chunking and sparse or dense indexing through reranking to grounded generation and evaluation, so each stage can be practised without running your own search infrastructure.
alternatives: pgvector keeps vectors inside an existing Postgres database, Qdrant and Weaviate are open-source vector databases you host yourself with built-in hybrid search, Elasticsearch and OpenSearch add vector search to a mature BM25 keyword engine, and LlamaIndex or LangChain are orchestration libraries that sit on top of any of these stores rather than replacing them.

setup.do: Read the four-stage description of a RAG system and sketch the offline ingestion half and the online retrieval half for a corpus you know.
setup.done_when: You have a one-page diagram naming the four stages and what data moves between them.
setup.why: Every later step fills in one box of this diagram, so you need the ingestion, retrieval, augmentation and generation split in your head first.

setup.do: Install the Pinecone Python SDK in a fresh virtual environment and pick your target: the free starter tier with an API key, or the Pinecone Local emulator in a container if you want no cloud account at all.
setup.done_when: A short script imports the SDK, connects and lists indexes without an error.

steps.done_when: A query returns ranked record ids with scores, and the top hit is the document you expected.

steps.why: This is the shortest route to a working retrieval round trip, and it shows the lexical side of search before embeddings are involved.

steps.do: Run the same five questions against the sparse index and against a dense index built with a free local embedding model, then combine the two result lists into one hybrid ranking.
steps.done_when: You have a table per question showing sparse, dense and hybrid top five, with at least one question where the hybrid list beats both.

steps.why: Hybrid search exists because exact terms such as product codes and names are found by sparse vectors while paraphrases are found by dense ones. Seeing each miss what the other finds makes the case concrete.

steps.do: Run your 20 questions twice through a small model, once closed-book using only what the model knows and once with retrieved passages added, and record both sets of answers.
steps.done_when: You can point at questions the closed-book run got wrong or refused and the retrieval run answered correctly.

steps.done_when: You have a hit-rate number for each chunking strategy and a written choice of which one to keep.

steps.why: Chunking decides what a single retrievable unit is, and persisting both variants side by side lets you compare them on the same questions instead of guessing.

steps.do: Write a contextual chunking pass that asks a model for a short situating sentence per chunk, prepends it before embedding, and load the result into a third namespace.
steps.done_when: At least one question that failed with plain chunks now retrieves the right chunk from the contextual namespace.

steps.why: Chunks cut out of a long document lose the context that says what they are about. Contextual retrieval restores it and usually rescues questions that plain chunks miss.

steps.do: Configure the dense index deliberately: choose the similarity metric that matches your embedding model, attach metadata such as source and date to every record, and query with a metadata filter.
steps.done_when: A filtered query returns only records from the chosen source and the scores are consistent with the metric you set.

steps.why: The metric and the filtering behaviour are properties of the vector index itself, and a wrong metric or missing metadata silently degrades every query built on it.

steps.do: Create a backup or collection of the winning index and restore it under a versioned name as your promoted index. If your tier or the local emulator does not offer backups, re-ingest into a new versioned index as the substitute.
steps.done_when: Two indexes exist with version names and the promoted one returns the same top results as the original.

steps.why: Treating an index as a versioned artifact lets you promote a known-good build and roll back when a new chunking or embedding change makes retrieval worse.

steps.do: Run a reranker over the top 25 hybrid results for each question and keep only the best few passages for the context window. Use the hosted rerank endpoint on the free tier or a small open reranker model on CPU.
steps.done_when: For several questions the relevant passage moves into the top three after reranking, and your context holds fewer passages than before.

steps.why: First-stage search is tuned for recall and a reranker restores precision, which lets you pass fewer and better passages to the model and keep the context window small.

steps.do: Write the generation prompt so the model answers only from the supplied passages, cites the passage id for each claim and says it does not know when the passages are insufficient.
steps.done_when: Answers carry passage ids you can trace to stored chunks, and an out-of-corpus question gets an explicit do-not-know reply.

source.title: RAG makes LLMs better and equal | Pinecone

steps.why: Grounded generation is what makes an answer checkable, and the refusal instruction is what stops the model from falling back to unsupported parametric knowledge.

steps.do: Create an evaluation run that scores your 20 questions on retrieval hit rate and on answer faithfulness and relevancy, and store the scores next to the index version.
steps.done_when: You have a results file with a retrieval score and an answer score per question for the promoted index.

source.title: RAG makes LLMs better and equal | Pinecone

steps.why: Most RAG quality problems are retrieval problems, so you need separate numbers for retrieval and for generation to know which half to fix.

steps.do: Write one script with pinned dependency versions that rebuilds the index from the raw documents, covering parse, chunk, embed and upsert, and then reruns the evaluation. Run it from a clean environment.
steps.done_when: A clean checkout plus one command produces a fresh index and evaluation scores within a small margin of your earlier run.
steps.why: An ingestion pipeline that only works from your notebook history cannot be rerun in CI or handed to a customer team. Rebuilding from scratch proves the result is reproducible.

steps.do: Configure a production-like layout: one namespace per tenant, a much larger corpus loaded through the pipeline, and latency measured for filtered queries under concurrent requests. Real scale needs a paid cloud plan, so use the free tier or local emulator with as many records as it allows.
steps.done_when: Queries for one tenant never return another tenant's records, and you have recorded median and tail latency at your largest corpus size.
